caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Angola's debt trajectory tracks the oil cycle with a lag. From 16.7% of GDP in 2006 it was contained through the boom, but the 2014 crash and kwanza depreciation drove it from 35.4% (2014) to a crushing 119.8% of GDP in 2020, the series high, with much of it dollar-linked Chinese and Eurobond debt. The December 2018 IMF Extended Fund Facility (about $3.7 billion) anchored fiscal consolidation, debt reprofiling, and exchange-rate flexibility; combined with the 2021-22 oil rebound, debt fell sharply to 57.3% in 2022. Another oil-price and currency wobble pushed it back to 75.6% in 2023 before easing to a projected 50.9% in 2025. Sustainability has improved but remains hostage to oil and the kwanza.
inflation_management: Angola's inflation is a mirror of the oil price and the kwanza. It ran in double digits through the boom (12-14% in 2006-2011), then fell to a series low of 7.3% in 2014 as oil peaked. The 2014 oil crash forced repeated kwanza devaluations and, in 2018, a shift toward a more flexible exchange rate under the IMF program; inflation exploded to 30.7% in 2016 and 29.8% in 2017. Tighter policy under the 2018 IMF arrangement brought it down to 17.1% by 2019, but shocks kept coming: 22.3% in 2020, 25.8% in 2021, and after another kwanza slide in 2023, inflation surged again to 28.2% in 2024, easing to a projected 20.2% in 2025. The central bank has hiked rates aggressively at each turn, but pass-through from the exchange rate dominates outcomes.

key_events.event: Oil price crash: GDP in USD terms peaked at $164.4bn (2014) then collapsed; debt and inflation surged.
Joao Lourenco succeeded Jose Eduardo dos Santos after 38 years, launching an anti-corruption drive (Isabel dos Santos assets frozen in the 2020 'Luanda Leaks' fallout).
IMF approved a three-year Extended Fund Facility of about $3.7 billion (December 7, 2018); kwanza moved to a more flexible regime.
COVID-19 and an oil price collapse pushed debt to 119.8% of GDP, the series peak; IMF augmented the program.
Lourenco narrowly won re-election; oil rebound cut debt to 57.3% of GDP.
Kwanza slide and OPEC production cuts re-accelerated debt and inflation (28.2% in 2024).

outlook_next_decade: The base case is oil-dependent stabilization: with the IMF program completed and debt back near 50% of GDP, Angola has breathing room, but another oil downturn would quickly reverse it. Upside depends on diversification and the long-promised new oil licensing rounds offsetting declining mature fields; downside is kwanza volatility reigniting the inflation-debt spiral. Uncertainty is moderate-to-high given oil concentration and the opacity of Chinese bilateral debt.
